questions.question_text: Under SDCL 43-4-44, the seller's property condition disclosure applies to which properties?
questions.correct_answer: Residential real property of 1 to 4 units
distractors: All real property regardless of type
Commercial properties over 5,000 square feet
Only single-family detached homes
questions.explanation: The statement is required for residential real property of no more than four dwelling units, all contained in one structure (SDCL 43-4-37). It applies whether the seller uses an agent or sells the property directly.

questions.question_text: When must the seller provide the property condition disclosure to the buyer?
questions.correct_answer: Before the buyer makes a written offer
distractors: Within 5 days after contract acceptance
At the time of the home inspection
At closing, before signing final documents
questions.explanation: The completed statement must reach the buyer before the buyer makes a written offer (SDCL 43-4-38). If a material fact changes before closing or possession, the seller must deliver a written amendment disclosing it.

questions.question_text: A bank is selling a foreclosed residential property. Must the bank provide a seller's property condition disclosure?
questions.correct_answer: No, foreclosure sales are exempt from disclosure
distractors: Yes, all residential sales require disclosure
No, but only if the property is vacant
Yes, banks must disclose all known defects
questions.explanation: Foreclosure sales are exempt, along with court-ordered transfers, transfers to a mortgagee by a defaulting mortgagor, fiduciary transfers, transfers between co-owners, transfers to close relatives, and newly built homes never occupied (SDCL 43-4-43).

questions.question_text: A buyer makes a written offer and only then receives the seller's property condition disclosure statement by hand. What can the buyer do?
questions.correct_answer: Terminate the offer within three days
distractors: Terminate the offer within ten days
Nothing — the offer is already binding
Demand a price reduction equal to the repair cost
questions.explanation: A disclosure statement or material amendment delivered after the buyer's written offer lets the buyer terminate by written notice within three days of hand delivery, or six days if it arrived by mail (SDCL 43-4-39).

questions.question_text: A seller intentionally conceals a known foundation crack and does not disclose it. What liability may the seller face?
questions.correct_answer: Actual damages, repair costs, and attorney fees
distractors: A maximum fine of $5,000 from the SDREC
No liability if the buyer had an inspection
Criminal charges for fraud and deception
questions.explanation: A seller who intentionally or negligently violates the disclosure requirements owes the buyer actual damages and repairs, and the court may award costs and attorney fees to the prevailing party (SDCL 43-4-42). Completing the form truthfully shields the seller on disclosed defects.

questions.question_text: SB 171 (2025) added two questions to South Dakota's property condition disclosure form. What do they ask about?
questions.correct_answer: Whether the property is historically designated or in a historic district
distractors: Whether a previous owner of the property died there of natural causes
The price the seller originally paid and the current mortgage balance
Whether the property has previously been listed for sale by another brokerage
questions.explanation: The form asks whether a local governing body has designated the property historic under SDCL 1-19B-20, and whether it sits within an established historic district. SB 171 (2025) added both questions, since designation can limit exterior alterations.

questions.question_text: The disclosure form asks whether the property has ever had water standing in the front, rear, or side yard. For how long?
distractors: More than 24 hours
More than 10 days
Any standing water at all
questions.explanation: The form asks whether the property has ever had water in the front, rear, or side yard for more than forty-eight hours (SDCL 43-4-44). It runs with the flood plain and wetlands questions, catching drainage a buyer would miss in dry weather.

questions.question_text: A seller knows of an unrecorded lien against the property. Does the disclosure form ask about it?
questions.correct_answer: Yes — the form asks about unrecorded liens too
distractors: No — only recorded liens appear on the form
No — unrecorded liens are the title company's job
Yes — but only if a lawsuit is already pending
questions.explanation: The form asks separately about recorded liens and about unrecorded liens or financial instruments, in both cases other than a first mortgage (SDCL 43-4-44). The unrecorded item also catches materials or services furnished in the past 120 days that could ripen into a lien.

questions.question_text: A seller disclosed a cracked foundation on the statement. After closing the buyer sues over that crack. Is the seller liable?
questions.correct_answer: No — truthful disclosure shields the seller on that defect
distractors: Yes, the seller warrants the condition either way
Yes, unless the buyer also had an inspection
Only if the repair exceeds the purchase price by 10 percent
questions.explanation: A seller who truthfully completes the disclosure statement is not liable for a defect or condition disclosed in it (SDCL 43-4-40). The statement is not a warranty; it is a record of what the seller knew, and disclosing in good faith is what earns the protection.

questions.question_text: A seller subject to the disclosure statute never delivers the statement, and the sale closes anyway. What is the effect on the transfer?
questions.correct_answer: The sale stands; the buyer's remedy is damages and repairs
distractors: The sale is void and the buyer's deposit must be returned
The sale is voidable at the buyer's option for one year
The sale stands and the buyer has no remedy once title passes
questions.explanation: A transfer subject to the disclosure statute is not invalidated solely because a person fails to comply (SDCL 43-4-42). Title passes and stays passed; the buyer's recourse is an action for actual damages and repairs, not undoing the conveyance.
